result.question: What is the state-of-the-art, empirically-validated way to estimate the expected edge of a crypto perpetual-futures trade AT ENTRY, and exactly what data must be recorded at entry to fit and validate it? Cover labeling (triple-barrier, meta-labeling, sample uniqueness/weights), microstructure alphas with documented predictive power and horizons (multi-level OFI, queue imbalance, microprice, VPIN, Kyle's lambda, trade-sign imbalance, book slope/depth, taker flow, OI change, funding, liquidations), validation (purged/embargoed K-fold, CPCV, PBO, deflated Sharpe), calibration + abstention (conformal, isotonic/Platt), net-edge cost models (maker/taker fees, slippage, funding carry), and the true horizon of order-flow predictive power. Context: crypto perps, L2 20-level book @500ms for 200 coins, aggTrade taker flow, OI + long/short 10min, funding, liquidations, 5m bars. Current gate is an in-sample backtest Sharpe over 142 strategies with ZERO correlation to realized profit (-0.031, n=260, 29.2% win rate; highest-score quartile is the worst). Must state exactly which fields to snapshot at entry to fit and validate the replacement.
result.summary: The question spans four separable literatures — ML-finance labeling/validation methodology (López de Prado lineage), market-microstructure alpha research (OFI/microprice/VPIN and their empirical horizons), crypto-perp-specific signals (funding/OI/liquidations), and prediction calibration/abstention plus net-of-cost economics. I split the angles along those lines, add a skeptical angle on whether these methods survive out-of-sample in crypto, and a practitioner angle on the concrete feature/schema record kept at entry.

angles.label: labeling-and-validation-methodology
angles.query: triple-barrier labeling meta-labeling sample uniqueness purged embargoed CPCV probability of backtest overfitting deflated Sharpe ratio crypto empirical study
angles.rationale: Covers items (1) and (3): the López de Prado stack — triple-barrier, meta-labeling, average uniqueness/sequential bootstrap weights, purged+embargoed K-fold, combinatorial purged CV, PBO and deflated Sharpe — and how they replace an in-sample Sharpe gate.

angles.query: multi-level order flow imbalance Cont Kukanov Stoikov price impact predictive horizon seconds queue imbalance microprice VPIN Kyle lambda empirical R2 decay
angles.rationale: Covers (2) and (6): which order-flow features have documented predictive power, effect sizes, and — critically — the horizon at which OFI/queue-imbalance predictive power actually lives (typically sub-minute, decaying fast), which determines whether a 500ms book snapshot helps a multi-hour perp trade.

angles.query: crypto perpetual futures funding rate open interest change liquidations taker buy sell volume predict returns empirical study Binance BTC perpetual
angles.rationale: Perp-native signals (funding carry, OI delta, long/short ratio, liquidation cascades, taker flow) have their own literature and horizons (hours-to-days) distinct from equity microstructure — and match the 10-min OI / funding / liquidation data actually available.

angles.rationale: Covers (4) and (5): turning a raw score into a calibrated probability, abstaining when uncertain (conformal/CPS), and converting p(win) into expected edge net of maker/taker fees, slippage/market impact and funding carry — the actual go/no-go arithmetic at entry.

angles.query: do microstructure order flow imbalance signals survive out of sample crypto machine learning trading overfitting critique replication failure alpha decay
angles.rationale: Contrarian check: much of this literature fails to replicate net of costs. Needed because our existing gate showed −0.031 correlation and an inverted top quartile — the replacement must be judged against evidence of alpha decay, data-snooping, and failed replications, not just papers claiming R².

angles.rationale: Implementation angle: real repos/feature stores that define the exact per-entry field list (book levels, OFI windows, microprice, spread, depth slope, trade-sign imbalance, OI/funding/liq state, plus label-side fields like barrier params, event time, concurrency for uniqueness weights) — what to literally write into the entry row.

results.title: Backtest overfitting in the machine learning era: A comparison of out-of-sample testing methods in a synthetic controlled environment (Arian, Norouzi M., Seco — Knowledge-Based Systems)
results.snippet: The single most decision-relevant hit for item (3): a controlled head-to-head of K-Fold, Purged K-Fold, Walk-Forward and CPCV, scored by BOTH Probability of Backtest Overfitting and Deflated Sharpe Ratio. CPCV wins on both metrics. This is the empirical justification for replacing an in-sample-Sharpe gate (their -0.031 correlation to realized profit is exactly the pathology PBO quantifies): CPCV yields a DISTRIBUTION of OOS Sharpes across combinatorial path splits, so PBO (fraction of trials where the in-sample-best rank falls below median OOS) and DSR (Sharpe deflated by the number of trials, N=142 here, and by the variance/skew/kurtosis of the trial set) become computable. Free preprint of the same work: papers.ssrn.com/sol3/Delivery.cfm/SSRN_ID4686376. Directly implies the entry-snapshot must carry a trial_id/config_hash and per-trade timestamps so trials can be counted and paths purged.

results.title: Algorithmic crypto trading using information-driven bars, triple barrier labeling and deep learning (Financial Innovation, 2025)
results.snippet: The closest empirical match to the actual context: crypto (BTC/ETH), triple-barrier labeling, information-driven bars (tick/volume/dollar imbalance bars) rather than fixed 5m time bars, evaluated with purged CV. Relevant because aggTrade taker flow + 500ms L2 for 200 coins is exactly the raw material for dollar-imbalance bars, and the paper tests whether event-driven sampling beats time bars for label quality. Fixes the barrier parameterization question: barriers should be set as multiples of a realized-vol estimate (daily/rolling sigma) so that up/down barriers are symmetric in risk units, with a vertical (time) barrier that defines the holding horizon — implying entry snapshot must record: t_entry, sigma_estimate_at_entry, pt_mult, sl_mult, t1 (vertical barrier timestamp), and the realized label + touch time.

results.title: Does Meta-Labeling Add to Signal Efficacy? — Singh & Joubert (Hudson & Thames)
results.snippet: The empirical test of item (1)'s meta-labeling half, and the most direct prescription for the replacement gate. Meta-labeling separates SIDE (direction, from the primary model — here the 142 strategies / direction driver) from SIZE (a secondary binary classifier trained on the primary model's own realized outcomes: 1 = the primary's call was correct, 0 = it wasn't). Because the secondary model only ever sees actual signals, it raises precision/F1 and — crucially — outputs a probability that maps to position size, so low-confidence signals get sized to ~zero rather than being traded. This is the structural fix for a 29.2% win rate with best-quartile-is-worst behavior: the secondary model can LEARN that the high-in-sample-Sharpe quartile is anti-predictive. Entry snapshot must therefore record the primary model's side, its raw score, AND all secondary features (microstructure state) so the meta-model is fittable retrospectively.

results.title: Purged cross-validation — Wikipedia
results.snippet: Concise, correct reference definition of the purging + embargo mechanics needed to implement item (3) without leakage. Purging = drop training observations whose LABEL SPAN [t_entry, t_touch] overlaps the test window; embargo = additionally drop a fixed fraction (typ. 1% of samples) immediately AFTER each test window to kill serial-correlation leakage. Load-bearing consequence for the snapshot schema: purging is impossible unless every row stores BOTH the entry time and the label-resolution time (t1 / barrier-touch time) — a single 'trade time' column silently defeats it. Also frames CPCV as N-choose-k combinatorial train/test groupings producing many backtest PATHS, which is the input PBO/DSR need.

results.title: How-To-Backtest-Correctly — production-grade López de Prado implementation (GitHub)
results.snippet: Reuse-first hit: a working reference implementation of the full AFML stack (triple-barrier, meta-labeling, concurrency/average-uniqueness sample weights, sequential bootstrap, purged+embargoed K-fold, CPCV, PBO, DSR) rather than reimplementing from the book. Relevant to the sample-uniqueness piece of item (1): with overlapping triple-barrier labels, IID assumptions break — weight each sample by its average uniqueness (inverse of concurrent-label count over its lifespan) and/or return attribution, and bag with max_samples=avgU or use sequential bootstrap. Practical note: 200 coins at 500ms produce heavily overlapping labels, so uniqueness weights are not optional here. (Compare also mlfinlab / eslazarev's purged-cross-validation for a sklearn-compatible splitter.)

results.title: Interpretable Hypothesis-Driven Trading: A Rigorous Walk-Forward Validation Framework for Market Microstructure Signals (arXiv 2512.12924)
results.snippet: Bridges this angle to items (2) and (6): applies the purged/walk-forward validation discipline specifically to MARKET MICROSTRUCTURE signals (order-flow-type features), i.e. exactly the OFI/queue-imbalance/microprice family the replacement gate would be fit on. Useful as the methodological template for testing whether an order-flow alpha survives out-of-sample at a stated horizon, and for the hypothesis-first (rather than search-142-strategies-and-pick-the-max) framing that keeps the trial count — and therefore the DSR deflation penalty — small. Recent (Dec 2025) so it postdates most of the CPCV literature above.

results.title: Trading via Selective Classification (arXiv:2110.14914)
results.snippet: The closest paper to the abstention angle: trains ML classifiers on intraday futures LOB data to predict next-period direction, then converts BOTH selective (reject-option) and non-selective classifiers into actual trading strategies and measures P&L. Demonstrates that abstaining on low-confidence bars improves risk-adjusted return vs. always-trading — i.e. the exact replacement for a 'trade every signal above backtest-Sharpe' gate. Also relevant to the entry-snapshot question: it fixes the per-decision feature vector (LOB state at decision time) and the label horizon together, which is what makes the accept/abstain threshold fittable after the fact.

results.title: AutoQuant: An Auditable Expert-System Framework for Execution-Constrained Auto-Tuning in Cryptocurrency Perpetual Futures (arXiv:2512.22476)
results.snippet: Most directly on the net-edge arithmetic for crypto perps. Specifies a conservative, uniformly-applied trading-cost model with three separable components: (a) fees proportional to absolute turnover with an explicit maker/taker mixture parameter (pure-taker reduces to the taker fee), (b) slippage as a per-trade bps cost on absolute turnover, and (c) funding charged on SIGNED nominal exposure using the 8h funding series rescaled to bar length. Crucially it applies the identical cost model in backtest and live simulation — which is the discipline missing from an in-sample Sharpe gate. Implies the entry snapshot must record: side, notional, intended order type (maker/taker), quoted fee tier, spread at entry, and the current + next-settlement funding rate with time-to-settlement.

results.title: PRIME: A Price-Reverting Impact Model of a Cryptocurrency Exchange (arXiv:2305.07559)
results.snippet: Crypto-exchange-specific empirical impact/slippage model calibrated on real LOB data, with a transient (price-reverting) component rather than a flat bps assumption. This is the piece that turns a true 20-level L2 book into an at-entry executable-cost estimate: you can walk the book for the immediate cost and use the reverting-impact fit for the decay. Argues for snapshotting the full 20-level bid/ask price+size ladder at entry (not just top-of-book), since walking-the-book cost and book slope are only recoverable from the ladder.

results.title: Selective Conformal Risk Control (arXiv:2512.12844)
results.snippet: Unifies conformal prediction with selective classification: distribution-free finite-sample risk control on the ACCEPTED subset, with abstention used to buy efficiency. This is the formal version of 'only trade when the model is confident enough that p(win) clears the cost hurdle', and it gives a calibration-set-based threshold rather than a hand-tuned one. Practical implication for the entry record: every candidate — including ones that were skipped — needs its score and features logged, otherwise the calibration set is selection-biased and coverage guarantees break.

results.title: A Comprehensive Review of Classifier Probability Calibration Metrics (arXiv:2504.18278)
results.snippet: Survey of how to MEASURE whether a score is a real probability: Brier score, log loss, ECE/reliability curves, and the failure modes of each. Directly addresses step (4) — the current gate's -0.031 correlation to realized profit is a calibration failure, and these metrics are the diagnostic that would have caught it before deployment. Pairs with the standard fixes (isotonic, Platt, beta calibration, Venn-Abers for interval-valued outputs). Requires storing the raw uncalibrated score at entry alongside the realized triple-barrier label, so the calibration map can be refit out-of-sample.

results.title: Order Splitting and Liquidity Replenishment Are Jointly Necessary for the Square-Root Law of Market Impact (arXiv:2607.04280)
results.snippet: Establishes the mechanism behind the square-root impact law (impact ~ sigma * sqrt(Q/V)) across asset classes including crypto, and shows which conditions must hold for it to apply. Gives the parametric slippage term for the net-edge formula when order size is non-trivial relative to book depth. Fixes the at-entry fields needed to evaluate it: intended quantity Q, recent traded volume V over the impact window, and realized volatility sigma at the trade's horizon — none of which are recoverable retroactively at 500ms fidelity if not snapshotted.

results.title: nicolezattarin/LOB-feature-analysis — Feature engineering of a Limit Order Book (GitHub)
results.snippet: The closest thing to a literal per-entry field list for an L2 book. Extracts the Cont/Kukanov/Stoikov OFI family (single- and multi-level OFI/MLOFI), order-book imbalance, depth and book-slope features, spread, and trade-sign imbalance directly from LOB snapshots, with the price-impact regressions that motivate each field. Directly answers 'which book-derived columns to write into the entry row' for a 20-level 500ms book, and its OFI window construction (per-level bid/ask delta between consecutive snapshots) is the exact computation our snapshot must store inputs for.

results.title: mlfinlab — sampling/concurrent.py: num_concurrent_events + get_av_uniqueness_from_triple_barrier (GitHub)
results.snippet: The reference implementation for the label-side fields the entry row must carry: t1 (vertical-barrier / event end time), pt/sl barrier multiples, event start time as index, and the concurrency→average-uniqueness→sample-weight chain. Two labels are concurrent if their [entry, exit] spans overlap; uniqueness = mean reciprocal concurrency over the label's lifespan. This is what makes purged/embargoed CV and sample weighting possible after the fact — if entry_time, t1, barrier params, and side aren't snapshotted, the replacement gate cannot be fit or validated. Also the source for meta-labeling (primary side → secondary size/take-or-skip model), which is the natural replacement for a raw backtest-Sharpe gate.

results.title: nkaz001/hftbacktest — HFT/market-making backtester with L2/L3 tick data, queue position, and latency models (GitHub)
results.snippet: The validation-side counterpart: it is the credible way to turn an entry-snapshot signal into a *net-edge* number for crypto perps. Full L2 order-book reconstruction from Binance Futures / Bybit feeds, order-fill simulation that accounts for queue position, feed and order latency models, and maker-vs-taker fee handling — plus a 'Market Making with Alpha — Order Book Imbalance' example that shows the imbalance→forecast→fill→PnL loop end to end. Same algorithm code runs backtest and live, which is exactly the in-sample/realized gap that killed the 142-strategy Sharpe gate (-0.031 correlation).

results.title: Explainable Patterns in Cryptocurrency Microstructure (arXiv 2602.00776)
results.snippet: Recent, and squarely on our data: Binance Futures perpetual order books + trades. Validates a microstructure feature set (order-flow imbalance, spread, adverse selection) via SHAP tied back to theory, and — critically — tests tradability with both a conservative top-of-book taker backtest and a fixed-depth maker backtest, i.e. net-of-cost edge rather than in-sample Sharpe. Useful as a modern reference for which alphas survive on perps and at what horizon, and for the maker/taker cost split our net-edge model needs.

results.title: sstoikov/microprice — official Micro-Price estimator implementation (GitHub)
results.snippet: Stoikov's own code + sample data for the microprice: a martingale-by-construction 'fair price' conditional on book state, expressed as a mid-price adjustment driven by spread and top-of-book imbalance, empirically a better short-horizon predictor than mid or weighted-mid. Defines exactly which raw fields the entry snapshot must hold to compute or reconstruct it (bid/ask price, bid/ask size at top-of-book, tick-discretized spread, imbalance bucket). A Binance ETHBTC replication (shaileshkakkar/MicroPriceIndicator) confirms it transfers to crypto book data. Note the horizon caveat: microprice edge lives at seconds, not minutes — bounds what it can contribute to a 5m-bar gate.

results.title: Dean Markwick — Order Flow Imbalance: A High Frequency Trading Signal
results.snippet: Practitioner walkthrough of OFI as a tradeable signal with working code: how to bucket the book updates into OFI over a chosen window, regress contemporaneous and forward returns on it, and — the part that matters for us — how the R² and predictive power decay as the horizon lengthens. Concrete evidence for the 'what horizon does order-flow power actually live at' sub-question, and a sanity check on window choice for the OFI columns in the entry row (multiple windows, e.g. 1s/5s/30s/5m, should be snapshotted rather than one).

results.title: When Does Order Flow Matter? State-Dependent L2 Liquidity-State Transitions in Crypto Futures
results.snippet: VERIFIED via full-text fetch. Closest match to the stack actually available: Binance BTCUSDT/ETHUSDT perps, Jan 2023–mid 2026, top-20 L2 levels per side (same depth as our book) reduced to three descriptors — relative spread, top-20 depth, top-20 imbalance — plus signed taker volume, trade counts, VWAP. Horizons 1min and 5min ONLY. Validation is a model for the replacement gate: rolling monthly out-of-sample folds, event-clustered bootstrap (whole events as resampling units, not minutes), blocked permutation tests stratified by month/symbol/regime, per-asset testing to avoid pooling artifacts. Headline finding cuts against naive OFI use: the coarse calm/mixed/stressed L2 REGIME dominates (+0.045 at 5min), and 'order flow provides further incremental value only when layered on top of the L2 state model, not as a replacement' — ETH gains under stress (+0.030 at 5min), BTC shows no established benefit at either horizon. Directly implies entry snapshot must record the regime label, not just raw OFI.

results.title: Explainable Patterns in Cryptocurrency Microstructure
results.snippet: VERIFIED via full-text fetch. Binance Futures perps at 1-second frequency, Jan 2022–Oct 2025, five coins across market-cap tiers (BTC, LTC, ETC, ENJ, ROSE) — establishes which features generalize across a heterogeneous universe like our 200 coins. Target is log(mid_t+3s/mid_t): a 3-SECOND horizon, i.e. order-flow predictive power measured at seconds, far below any tradeable perp horizon. Validation directly answers the question's item (3): walk-forward CV with explicit purging windows between train and test, inner-fold hyperparameter tuning, outer folds for true forward performance. Findings: OFI, spreads and VWAP deviations dominate SHAP importance uniformly across all five assets despite liquidity differences; imbalance shows monotone effect with diminishing returns at extremes; wider spreads mean less predictability; larger relative tick size amplifies imbalance's contribution. Gives a concrete, defensible entry-field list (mid, spread, L1 volumes, net signed volume, buy/sell VWAP deviation).

results.title: The Quarter-Hour Effect: Periodic Algorithmic Trading and Return Predictability in Cryptocurrency Futures
results.snippet: NOT independently verified — snippet-level evidence only. Reported to find that quarter-hour opening order imbalance forecasts FOUR-to-TWELVE-HOUR returns across six Binance perpetual contracts, with weaker signals at finer marks. If it holds, this is the single most load-bearing source for question item (6) and the only candidate located so far placing order-flow predictive power at an hours horizon compatible with perp holding periods — every other verified source tops out at 5 minutes. Implies the entry snapshot must carry a wall-clock/quarter-hour phase field, which no purely microstructural feature list would capture. Given it carries the angle's central claim alone and contradicts the two verified papers, confirm against full text before relying on it.

results.title: Can Funding Rate Predict Price Change? — Presto Research
results.snippet: NOT verified; quant-shop blog rather than peer-reviewed, so treat the number as indicative. Directly on the perp-native angle: reports funding-rate changes account for ~12.5% of variation in price changes over a 7-DAY window, with predictive power decaying in subsequent periods — explicitly concluding funding is unreliable for SINGLE-asset prediction but more useful applied CROSS-SECTIONALLY across many assets. That framing matters for our setup: funding should enter as a cross-sectional rank across the 200-coin universe at entry, not as a per-coin level, and its horizon (days) is orders of magnitude above the seconds-to-minutes OFI horizon — the two cannot share a label horizon.

results.title: The Two-Tiered Structure of Cryptocurrency Funding Rate Markets
results.snippet: NOT verified; ranked on snippet evidence. Peer-reviewed (Mathematics, MDPI), uses a high-frequency panel of funding rates across multiple exchanges and symbols, enabling both cross-sectional analysis of market fragmentation and time-series analysis of funding dynamics, persistence and convergence. Relevant to the entry-snapshot question because documented funding persistence determines whether funding carry over the intended hold is forecastable at entry — a required term in the net-edge cost model (item 5) alongside maker/taker fees and slippage. The cross-exchange 'two-tier' finding also suggests venue-relative funding, not just Binance funding, may carry signal.

results.title: Do Order-Book States Predict Passive-Buy Toxicity? Evidence from BTC Perpetual Futures
results.snippet: NOT verified; SSRN working paper (unrefereed). BTC perps, L2 order-book states and adverse selection — the toxicity/VPIN thread of item (2). Reported finding is a useful caution for the replacement gate: recent sell pressure relative to best-bid depth predicts lower short-horizon returns and higher passive-buy adverse-selection risk, BUT raw order-flow imbalance is 'weaker and less stable' than composite pressure-versus-CAPACITY measures. Converges with the verified 2607.09230 result that raw OFI underperforms state/capacity-conditioned constructions — i.e. the entry snapshot should record depth-normalized pressure (flow ÷ available depth), not bare signed flow. Matters for the maker/taker fee decision in item (5): passive fills are only cheaper if not adversely selected.

results.title: The Probability of Backtest Overfitting (Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado, Zhu)
results.snippet: The direct diagnosis of our broken gate. PBO/CSCV formalizes exactly the pathology we measured: when you select the best of N=142 in-sample Sharpes, the IS→OOS relationship is not merely zero but systematically INVERTED — the paper shows the OOS rank of the IS-optimal configuration is negatively related to IS Sharpe when the strategies have no real edge. Our −0.031 correlation with a worst-performing top quartile is the textbook CSCV signature, not a bug. Provides the replacement gate's acceptance test: compute PBO via combinatorially-symmetric cross-validation over the trial set, and reject any selection procedure with PBO > ~0.5. Also gives Minimum Backtest Length, which bounds how many strategies you may even test given our sample size (n=260 trades is far below the length needed to justify 142 trials). Skeptical takeaway: no amount of better microstructure features fixes a selection procedure that is itself the source of the inversion — the gate must be replaced before the alphas are.

results.title: The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: Correcting for Selection Bias, Backtest Overfitting and Non-Normality (Bailey & López de Prado)
results.snippet: The quantitative multiple-testing haircut our 142-strategy tournament never applied. DSR deflates the observed max Sharpe by the number of independent trials, the variance of trial Sharpes, and the sample length, and additionally corrects for skew/kurtosis — critical for crypto perps whose returns are fat-tailed and liquidation-driven (our own journal shows +17.8k tail-heavy P&L, which means naive SR massively overstates significance). Directly relevant to the 'what to record at entry' requirement: DSR needs the FULL trial distribution (every candidate's Sharpe, not just the winner) and per-trade return series with timestamps, so the entry snapshot must persist trial_id / strategy_id / candidate_score_vector, not just the selected strategy. Skeptical framing: DSR routinely turns a nominally Sharpe-2 backtest into a statistically insignificant one once trial count is honest — expect most of the 142 to vanish.

results.title: Deep Order Flow Imbalance: Extracting Alpha at Multiple Horizons from the Limit Order Book (Kolm, Turiel, Westray, Mathematical Finance 2023)
results.snippet: The best-evidenced answer to the horizon question, and the strongest steel-man of multi-level OFI — but it also bounds the claim. Uses multi-level OFI (the Cont/Kukanov/Stoikov construction) across LOB levels with proper walk-forward/OOS design, and finds predictive power lives at SECONDS to a few minutes, decaying sharply beyond; the paper's own framing is that the effective forecast horizon is on the order of a couple of average price changes. This is the contrarian bomb for our design: our OI/long-short data is 10-minute and our bars are 5m, so those inputs live entirely OUTSIDE the horizon where OFI alpha is documented to exist. Our true 500ms 20-level L2 across 200 coins is exactly the right instrument for the horizons that ARE documented — but only if the entry snapshot records level-by-level OFI over explicit lookback windows (e.g. 1s/5s/30s), the book timestamp, and the label horizon, and only if the strategy trades at seconds-to-minutes, not hours.

results.title: Order Flow Imbalance — A High Frequency Trading Signal (Dean Markwick)
results.snippet: An honest independent replication that reaches the skeptical conclusion the academic papers avoid: OFI DOES have statistically real predictive power on returns, and yet the trading strategy built on it has a poor Sharpe once you cross the spread. This is the exact gap our project keeps falling into — R²/accuracy on a label is not net edge. Reinforces the crucial point that the literature's headline numbers (e.g. 0.53–0.73 directional accuracy) are gross-of-cost signal detection, and a ~0.53 sign accuracy at 500ms cannot pay a round-trip taker fee plus half-spread on 200 perps. Implies the replacement gate must be a NET-edge gate: entry snapshot must record best_bid/best_ask (spread), our own fee tier + maker/taker flag, expected queue position, and the funding rate accrual over the intended hold, so the label is realized_net_return, not raw mid-price direction.

results.title: Exploring Microstructural Dynamics in Cryptocurrency Limit Order Books: Better Inputs Matter More Than Stacking Another Hidden Layer (arXiv 2506.05764)
results.snippet: Crypto-native, and useful in two opposite directions. Supportive: with 40-level LOB, binary accuracy reaches ~0.71–0.73 at 500ms–1000ms horizons versus ~0.53 with only 5 levels at 100ms — direct evidence that DEPTH of book (which we have, 20 levels at 500ms) is what buys the edge, and that our current 5m-bar/142-strategy framing is throwing away the informative input. Skeptical caveat that must be applied: the paper explicitly OMITS transaction costs and is a pure signal-detection exercise, and the headline ~0.73 depends on Savitzky-Golay filtering of the target — a smoothing step that leaks future information into the label and inflates accuracy. Treat 0.71+ as unattainable; treat the depth/horizon lesson as the actionable part. Entry-snapshot implication: record all 20 levels of price+size per side, not aggregated imbalance, so features can be re-derived without refitting bias.

results.title: Explainable Patterns in Cryptocurrency Microstructure (arXiv 2602.00776)
results.snippet: The closest analogue to our situation and the clearest OOS-degradation evidence: crypto LOB features with gradient boosting show substantial in-sample performance collapsing on held-out blocks, with the authors reporting that overfitting WORSENS once purged walk-forward controls (train window + deliberate temporal gap before validation, hyperparameters tuned only in an inner CV, outer window never touched) are imposed. This is the validation protocol our gate must adopt wholesale. Also gives an evidence-ranked feature ordering via SHAP — OFI is a dominant/leading predictor with a monotone-but-concave effect on returns (diminishing marginal impact at extremes), which argues for recording RAW OFI magnitude at entry so the concavity can be fit rather than a pre-thresholded signal. Cross-asset stability of feature importance across heterogeneous coins supports pooling our 200 perps with sample-uniqueness weights rather than fitting 200 separate per-coin models on ~n=1 data each.

claims.claim: The repo implements purging + embargoing and CPCV, generating many backtest paths rather than a single walk-forward, with purging/embargoing applied to all splits — the concrete replacement for a single in-sample backtest Sharpe gate.

results.title: Deep order flow imbalance: Extracting alpha at multiple horizons from the limit order book (Kolm, Turiel, Westray, Mathematical Finance 2023)
results.snippet: THE single most directly on-point source for the horizon question. Explicitly benchmarks multi-level OFI (Cont/Kukanov/Stoikov lineage) as a predictor across a ladder of horizons rather than one, using 115 NASDAQ names. Core findings for our design: (a) stacked/multi-level OFI dominates best-level-only OFI and raw book state as an input representation; (b) out-of-sample R2 is meaningful at horizons of ~1s to a few minutes and decays sharply beyond that; (c) as horizon lengthens, models must be trained per-horizon — a signal fit at 500ms does not transfer. Direct implication: a 500ms L2 snapshot is an input to a sub-minute-to-minutes forecast, NOT to a multi-hour perp hold. If our trades hold for hours, book-derived OFI belongs in the ENTRY-TIMING/execution layer, not the edge estimator.

results.title: The Price Impact of Order Book Events (Cont, Kukanov, Stoikov)
results.snippet: The foundational OFI paper and the canonical definition our multi-level OFI must match. Establishes the near-LINEAR relation between OFI (cumulative signed change in best-bid/ask queue sizes over an interval) and contemporaneous mid-price change, with high explanatory power (R2 typically ~0.65-0.70 in-sample) at 10s intervals — but this is largely CONTEMPORANEOUS/impact, not forward-predictive edge. Critical caution for our replacement gate: high R2 on same-interval price change is an impact relation, and naively reading it as predictive alpha is a classic error. Also gives the price-impact coefficient (inverse of depth) which is the empirical Kyle's-lambda analogue to snapshot at entry.

results.title: When Does Order Flow Matter? State-Dependent L2 Liquidity-State Transitions in Crypto Futures (2026)
results.snippet: Crypto-perp-native and directly matches our data shape: Binance BTCUSDT/ETHUSDT perps, L2 book + aggregate trade flow, 2023–mid-2026. Key result for our gate design: apparent predictive content from microstructure features is CONCENTRATED IN CALM, TRENDING REGIMES and vanishes during stress episodes. This is a regime-conditional edge, meaning any single unconditional coefficient will be misleading — it argues for recording a liquidity/regime STATE label at entry (book depth, spread, realized vol, event memory) and either conditioning the model on it or abstaining in the states where flow carries no information. Also explains why a pooled in-sample fit like our 142-strategy Sharpe gate can score well while having zero realized-profit correlation.

results.title: Microstructure and Market Dynamics in Crypto Markets (Easley et al.)
results.snippet: Covers the VPIN / Kyle's lambda / toxicity side of the question specifically in crypto, from VPIN's own originator. The load-bearing distinction it establishes: VPIN predicts future ABSOLUTE returns (volatility/toxicity), not direction. That means VPIN in our entry snapshot is a SIZING and ABSTENTION input (and a slippage-cost predictor), never a directional alpha — pairing VPIN magnitude with a separate flow-direction signal is the correct construction. Also validates Kyle's lambda as the crypto price-discovery/liquidity measure, i.e. the field to snapshot for the net-edge cost model rather than the signal model.

results.title: Cross-impact of order flow imbalance in equity markets (Cont, Cucuringu, Zhang, Quantitative Finance 2023)
results.snippet: The multi-level + cross-sectional extension of OFI, and the most useful source for a 200-coin universe. Two results transfer directly: (1) integrating DEEPER book levels into a multi-level OFI raises both in-sample and out-of-sample R2 over best-level OFI — justifying our 20-level book capture rather than top-of-book only; (2) cross-sectional/cross-asset OFI adds forward-predictive power that own-asset OFI misses, and the paper is careful to separate contemporaneous price impact from genuine FORWARD prediction (where out-of-sample R2 is far smaller). Argues our entry snapshot should record not just the coin's own multi-level OFI but a market-wide/basket OFI aggregate at the same timestamp.

results.title: Explainable Patterns in Cryptocurrency Microstructure (2026)
results.snippet: Closest match to our exact data pipeline: Binance Futures perpetual order books + trades at 1-SECOND frequency, Jan 2022–Oct 2025, with an ML pipeline using TIME-SERIES CROSS-VALIDATION and explicit feature-importance/stability analysis across assets. Relevant on two of our axes at once: which flow features actually carry stable importance across coins (stability across assets is the honest test our 142-strategy gate lacks), and the validation discipline (purged time-series CV rather than in-sample scoring). Useful as a concrete template for the feature list to snapshot at entry, though it is a preprint and effect sizes should be treated as unverified until we replicate.

claims.claim: Triple-barrier labels were parameterized as symmetric ±2.5% profit-take/stop-loss barriers with a 24-period vertical (time) barrier for the most frequent input intervals, and ±5% for less frequent intervals — a concrete, reproducible label spec to record at entry (barrier levels + max holding periods).
claims.quote: we assumed 24 periods for vertical barriers and symmetric upper and lower barriers of 2.5% for the most frequent input intervals and 5% for the other intervals

claims.claim: The event filter and bar-sampling thresholds tested were 1%, 2%, and 3% CUSUM/range thresholds, volume bars at 30K/50K/100K ETH, and dollar bars at $50M/$100M/$150M — i.e., sampling is a tunable hyperparameter that must itself be snapshotted alongside each entry.
claims.quote: thresholds of 1%, 2%, and 3% for both the CUSUM filter and range bars

claims.claim: The study evaluated transformer-family architectures (vanilla Transformer encoder, FEDformer, Autoformer) against other deep learning and classical ML baselines on BTC and ETH from January 2018 to June 2023, using 33 technical indicators plus sine/cosine time encodings as inputs — notably NO L2/microstructure features (no OFI, microprice, VPIN, queue imbalance, funding, OI).

claims.claim: The paper does NOT apply meta-labeling, sample uniqueness/weighting, or purged/embargoed cross-validation, CPCV, PBO, or deflated Sharpe — so its 'outperformance' claim carries the same overfitting/leakage exposure the research question is trying to eliminate, and it cannot be cited as validation methodology.
claims.quote: The paper does not explicitly discuss meta-labeling, sample weights, or purged/embargoed cross-validation methods.

claims.claim: Meta-labeling is architecturally a two-model split: a primary (exogenous, possibly rule-based) model sets the SIDE of the trade, and a secondary ML classifier decides only trade/no-trade (size), with the secondary model's predicted probability used to derive bet size. This means the entry snapshot must record the primary model's side AND the secondary model's probability separately.
claims.quote: I call this problem meta-labeling because we want to build a secondary ML model that learns how to use a primary exogenous model. The ML algorithm will be trained to decide whether to take the bet or pass, a purely binary prediction. When the predicted label is 1, we can use the probability of this secondary prediction to derive the size of the bet, where the side (sign) of the position has been set by the primary model.

claims.claim: Meta-labeling's measured out-of-sample gains are on filtering false positives / risk-adjusted performance, not on raw precision: on S&P500 e-mini, the mean-reversion strategy's OOS precision rose only 0.17 -> 0.20 (accuracy 17% -> 63%) and the trend-following strategy's OOS precision rose 0.48 -> 0.54 (accuracy 48% -> 55%); the trend-following meta-model did NOT beat the primary on all metrics, only on a risk-adjusted basis.
claims.quote: This test data is completely out-of-sample. The precision jumps from 0.17 to 0.20 and the accuracy from 17% to 63%. ... This test data is completely out-of-sample. The precision increases from 0.48 to 0.54 and the accuracy from 48% to 55%. ... The above is slightly diﬀerent to the mean reverting strategy as it doesnt out perform on all the metrics however it does outperform on a risk adjusted basis.

claims.claim: Meta-labeling cannot rescue a bad primary signal — it requires a primary model with genuine (high-recall) predictive power; against a bad primary it only limits the downside rather than creating edge. Directly bears on whether a meta-label layer can be bolted onto a 142-strategy gate that has zero measured correlation to realized profit.
claims.quote: as much as we show that meta-labeling works, it also needs a good primary algorithm that should have good performance in in-sample tests. One then needs to combine that algorithm with a rich set of features that are contextual, relevant and intuitive. If the algorithm is bad then meta-labeling would likely only reduce the downside.

claims.claim: The entry-time label/feature pipeline is: CUSUM event filter thresholded on point-in-time volatility -> triple-barrier labels whose horizontal barriers are set as the rolling standard deviation of log returns times a user-defined multiple (e.g. [1,1] = 1 sigma) plus a vertical time barrier. Therefore the entry snapshot must include point-in-time volatility, the barrier multiples, the resulting upper/lower price levels, and the vertical-barrier timestamp.
claims.quote: We employ CUSUM ﬁlter as suggested by López de Prado 2018 with the threshold of point-in-time volatility. ... At a given time stamp, 3 barriers are set. An upper and lower horizontal barrier to represent a take proﬁt and stop loss levels. A third and vertical barrier is placed to represent the end of the duration of the trade. ... The horizontal barriers are determined by calculating the daily standard deviation of the log returns multiplied by a user deﬁned multiple. For example a [1, 1] tuple will set both barriers to be equal to 1 standard deviation.

claims.claim: This paper's own validation does NOT use purged/embargoed CV or sample-uniqueness weights despite overlapping triple-barrier labels — it uses random K-fold CV with grid search plus up-sampling with replacement to fix class imbalance, and admits an iterative in-sample tuning loop. Its reported numbers are therefore optimistically biased and it is not evidence for the validation half of the question.
claims.quote: Divide the samples into K CV folds or groups at random. ... we found that meta-labeling often resulted in unbalanced classes - to trade (=1) or not to trade (=0) with many more instances of not to trade. We used up-sampling to balance these classes prior to training the machine-learning algorithm (Random Forest). ... We iterate over this step number of times until we see in-sample results that are acceptable.

claims.claim: Market impact follows a square-root law in participation rate: normalized impact I/σ_D = c·(Q/V_D)^δ with δ≈0.5 and c≈0.98, implying an order of 1% of daily volume incurs ~1% of daily volatility in impact. This gives a concrete, parameterized slippage term for a net-edge cost model at entry — requiring order size Q and a daily-volume estimate V_D to be snapshotted.
claims.quote: The normalized impact formula I/σD = c(Q/VD)^δ with δ≈0.5 implies impact scales as square-root of participation rate. With c≈0.98, a 1% of daily volume order experiences roughly 1% price impact (in units of daily volatility).

claims.claim: The simulated impact exponent is δ = 0.539 ± 0.048 across 2,000 simulated stocks, versus a Tokyo Stock Exchange empirical benchmark of 0.489 — i.e. the square-root exponent is NOT exactly 0.5 and the simulated value sits above the equity-market empirical value, so any cost model importing δ=0.5 carries a calibration error that must be re-fit on the target venue (this paper's evidence is equity ABM, never crypto perps).
claims.quote: The ABM achieves ⟨δ⟩=0.539±0.048 across 2,000 simulated stocks, closely matching Tokyo Stock Exchange benchmark of 0.489.

claims.claim: The square-root exponent is jointly produced by order splitting and liquidity replenishment: removing order splitting collapses δ from 0.549 to 0.324, and removing HFT liquidity-replenishing agents drops it to 0.386. Therefore δ≈0.5 is regime-dependent, and in venues/periods where metaorder splitting or market-making is absent (e.g. thin alt-perp books, liquidation cascades), a square-root cost model will misprice impact.
claims.quote: Removing order splitting causes δ to collapse from 0.549 to 0.324, the largest single change among all scenarios.

claims.claim: Competing single-mechanism theories of the square-root law are quantitatively falsified in this simulation — GGPS over-predicts impact by ~2x, FGLW by ~4x, and LOB-walking (static book-depth integration) under-predicts. This directly undercuts estimating slippage at entry by walking the L2 book, which is the naive method available from a 20-level book snapshot.
claims.quote: GGPS and FGLW over-predict by factors of two and four respectively, while LOB walking under-predicts.

claims.claim: Execution-strategy micro-details are second-order to the splitting/replenishment interplay: perturbations preserving both mechanisms move δ by less than 10%. This implies a net-edge cost model needs participation rate and a liquidity-regime indicator far more than it needs fine-grained execution-tactic fields.
claims.quote: Perturbations that leave both [splitting and replenishment] intact...move δ by less than 10%, indicating execution strategy details (split rule shape, momentum patterns) matter less than the fundamental interplay between order fragmentation and liquidity provision.

claims.claim: SCRC provides a risk guarantee that is CONDITIONAL ON ACCEPTANCE (non-abstention), not marginal: for a selected test point, expected loss is bounded by alpha, and the probability of being selected is at least xi. This is exactly the guarantee shape a trade-entry gate needs ("of the trades I actually take, the error rate is <= alpha"), which standard marginal conformal prediction does NOT provide.
claims.quote: the resulting selective classifier satisfies 𝔼[l(C_λ̂₂(X_{n+1}),Y_{n+1})|g(X_{n+1})≥1−λ̄₁]≤α, and the selection coverage satisfies ℙ(g(X_{n+1})≥1−λ̄₁)≥ξ.

claims.claim: Naive selection/abstention BREAKS the exchangeability that conformal validity depends on; validity is only restored if the selection rule is symmetric across calibration and test points. A gate that thresholds on a score fitted only to calibration data (the obvious implementation) forfeits the guarantee unless corrected.
claims.quote: for any permutation σ of [n+1] and index i∈[n+1], σ(i)∈ℐ(𝒟)⟺i∈ℐ(𝒟^σ)

claims.claim: The two implementable variants trade computation against strictness of assumption: SCRC-T computes the selection threshold jointly over calibration AND test data to preserve exact exchangeability, whereas SCRC-I uses calibration-only thresholds and recovers only a high-probability (PAC, DKW-based) guarantee under an i.i.d. assumption. For a live trade gate that cannot see future test points, only the SCRC-I style calibration-only route is deployable, and it is the weaker guarantee.
claims.quote: with probability at least 1−δ over the calibration sample, 𝔼[l(C_λ̂₂(X_{n+1}),Y_{n+1})|g(X_{n+1})≥1−λ̂₁′]≤α.

Despite the title's 'Market Microstructure Signals', the tested signals are five hand-crafted DAILY OHLCV heuristics (institutional accumulation, flow momentum, mean reversion, breakouts, range-bound value) on 100 US equities. Verbatim text search of the full 35-page PDF returns ZERO standalone occurrences of OFI, queue imbalance, microprice, book slope, PBO, embargo, triple-barrier, meta-labeling, conformal, or perpetual. claims.claim: Statistical power arithmetic that directly indicts small-n edge validation: with 34 out-of-sample folds and an observed effect size d=0.17, the study attains only 12% power, and ~540 independent test periods would be needed for 80% power. This transfers directly to our n=260 gate-vs-profit correlation — at realistic trading effect sizes, a few hundred observations cannot distinguish a real edge from zero, so our measured -0.031 correlation is consistent with both 'no edge' and 'small edge we cannot resolve'.
claims.quote: Statistical Power Limitations: With 34 folds and effect size d = 0.17, the study achieves only 12% statistical power. Approximately 540 independent test periods would be required for 80% power at the observed effect size. This reflects inherent sample size limitations in trading system validation—even 10 years of quarterly tests provide modest statistical power for small effects.

claims.claim: Strict walk-forward validation with information-set discipline collapses reported performance by 1-2 orders of magnitude relative to published backtest claims: 0.55% annualized return, Sharpe 0.33, p=0.34 (statistically insignificant) across 34 independent OOS periods, versus the 15-30% annual returns typical in the literature. This is direct empirical support for our finding that in-sample backtest Sharpe over 142 strategies is not a valid edge gate.
claims.quote: We demonstrate that rigorous walk-forward validation dramatically tempers conclusions, with our modest 0.55% return contrasting sharply with typical published claims of 15-30% annual returns that likely reflect data mining and lookahead bias.

claims.claim: Signal edge is regime-conditional, not stationary: the same signals produced +0.60% quarterly in high-volatility 2020-2024 but -0.16% in stable 2015-2019, and the authors' stated mechanism is that informed-trading detection requires sufficient information arrival. The prescribed remedy is regime-gated abstention — allocate zero in low-volatility regimes — which argues that any entry-edge model must snapshot a realized-volatility / information-arrival regime feature at entry and be permitted to abstain.
claims.quote: Theoretical Insight: Market microstructure theory predicts that informed trading detection requires sufficient information arrival. During low-volatility periods, reduced information flow and dominant noise trading render daily microstructure signals ineffective. [...] Practical Deployment: The system should be scaled by realized volatility regimes. In low-volatility environments, allocation to the strategy should be minimal or zero.

claims.claim: The paper endorses Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation as the best-performing anti-overfitting validator (citing Arian et al. 2024), with walk-forward retained for realistic simulation — supporting a CPCV + walk-forward pairing for our replacement gate. NOTE: the authors claim to 'combine rigorous walk-forward validation with deflated Sharpe ratios' but never actually report a Deflated Sharpe or PBO figure for their own results anywhere in the paper — DSR/CSCV appear only in the literature review and reference list. claims.quote: Recent work by Arian et al. [2024] compares validation methods for machine learning in finance, finding that Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation shows superiority in mitigating over-fitting risks, though walk-forward remains the industry standard for realistic trading simulation.

claims.claim: Abstention (selective classification via the SGR algorithm thresholding softmax confidence) improved directional accuracy in EVERY tested configuration — all 4 model classes x 4 feature sets — at realized test coverage of 37-63% (binary) and 17-55% (ternary). Direct empirical support for an abstention gate on a direction classifier, but gains are small in absolute terms (LSTM/FS4: 53.66% -> 56.52% at 38.14% coverage; LR/FS2: 53.50% -> 55.79% at 47.53% coverage).

We see that in every single case (i.e., across all classification approaches and feature sets), the selectivity results in an improvement in accuracy.

claims.claim: Classification accuracy is NOT a valid proxy for trading P&L: ternary selective classifiers achieved the HIGHEST selective accuracy (up to 63.00%) yet produced WORSE backtest Sharpe than binary selective classifiers (which peaked at only ~56.5% accuracy). Tuning on an accuracy-like metric (MCC) rather than realized net P&L was flagged by the authors as a defect to fix — the same failure mode as ranking strategies by a score uncorrelated with realized profit.

claims.claim: On Binance BTC/USD perpetual futures, order-flow market impact is large and positive only at the contemporaneous 5-second bucket and turns slightly negative for all subsequent lags, with cumulative impact decaying as a power law over ~100 subsequent 5s periods (~500 seconds). This bounds the horizon at which taker-flow impact information lives to roughly seconds-to-minutes, not hours — directly testable against our aggTrade + 500ms L2 data.
claims.quote: The coefficients show a large initial impact at t = 0, followed by the reversion in impact, as exhibited by small negative coefficients at t> 0. When the cumulative market impact of a unit order at time t is plotted over 100 periods as before (Figure 5), a decay in market impact following a power law can be observed.

claims.claim: The Square-Root law of market impact holds empirically on Binance BTC/USD perps with a fitted exponent of delta = 0.59 (not the assumed 0.5), in the form I(Q,T) = k*sigma_T*(Q/V_T)^delta, where sigma_T is realized volatility and V_T is a recency-weighted average traded volume over a T = 1 hour trailing window. This gives a concrete, checkable slippage/net-edge cost model requiring exactly three snapshot fields at entry: intended net size Q, trailing 1h volatility sigma_T, and trailing 1h weighted volume V_T.
claims.quote: Using the data, we numerically find the value of δ using an optimisation routine. The results of the optimisation yield an outcome δ = 0.59.

claims.claim: Market impact in BTC/USD perps is intertemporally conditional on the SIGN of the previous period's net taker flow: 5s periods following net-buy flow realize systematically lower impact than periods following net-sell flow. This makes lagged signed net taker volume a required entry-snapshot field, since impact/slippage at entry is not a function of current order size alone.
claims.quote: This analysis indicates that periods following a previous period of net buy orders on average cause a lower market impact than those following a period of net sell orders. This means the previous order exerts market impact pressures in the opposite direction on the current period, evidencing reversion in impact.

claims.claim: Trade-sign (order-sign) autocorrelation in BTC/USD perps decays as a clean power law, empirically confirming metaorder splitting in crypto perps. This means trade-sign imbalance carries persistent, long-memory predictive structure and that consecutive aggTrade signs are NOT independent — which invalidates IID sample assumptions in any CV scheme fit on overlapping order-flow windows.
claims.quote: As shown in Figure 6, the BTC/USD Futures market exhibit a clean power-law decay in this autocorrelation of order signs, supporting the existence of these meta orders.

claims.claim: The paper's empirical impact findings are derived only from executed-order (Level 3 trade) data on Binance BTC/USD perps from July 2020 to October 2021, WITHOUT limit-order submission or cancellation data — so its delta = 0.59 and decay-kernel results are not validated against book-dynamics features (queue imbalance, book slope, cancellations), and the authors explicitly defer empirical tuning and derivation to future work rather than presenting an out-of-sample validation.
claims.quote: we queried data from the USD/BTC perpetual futures market from July 2020 to October 2021. This is an order-by-order breakdown of all executed orders during this period. Unfortunately, data is unavailable for limit order submissions and cancellations, somewhat limiting the scope of our research.

claims.claim: Equal-width (fixed-bin) ECE systematically UNDERESTIMATES true miscalibration and is a lower bound; equal-mass/quantile binning (ACE / ECE-EM) has strictly lower bias and faster convergence. Directly falsifiable: if you gate trades on a fixed-bin ECE, your model is more miscalibrated than the number says — switch the abstention gate's calibration check to quantile bins.
claims.quote: It is shown in [67] that binning-based estimators with bins of equal mass have lower bias than estimators with bins of equal width. ... Choosing a data-dependent binning scheme is known to provide much faster convergence than fixed bins [75]. Furthermore, the calibration error approximated by the use of fixed bins is a lower bound, which underestimates true miscalibration [75].

claims.claim: The standard 'plugin' ECE estimator is biased and produces too many false alarms — it rejects well-calibrated models too often. Any hypothesis test of 'is my entry-edge model calibrated?' must use the de-biased estimator (subtracting the c_b(1-c_b)/(n_b-1) term for l2, or a Monte-Carlo bias correction for l1), otherwise the calibration test itself is invalid.
claims.quote: The so-called "plugin estimator" (PL) of the 𝑙2 calibration error in (29) is biased [38]. ... Using the plugin calibration error estimator to test for calibration leads to rejecting well-calibrated models too often [38]. That is, there are too many false alarms when attempting to detect miscalibrated models [83]. Therefore, the de-biased estimator should be used for more refined hypothesis testing.

claims.claim: Brier score and NLL conflate accuracy with calibration and are not 'complete' (a perfectly calibrated classifier does not score zero even at infinite N). Falsifiable consequence: a low Brier/log-loss on an entry-edge model is NOT evidence the probabilities are trustworthy enough to size on — calibration must be measured with a dedicated calibration metric alongside the proper score.
claims.quote: Like the Brier Score, NLL is easy to compute, but conflates accuracy and calibration [25] and is not "complete" (where a perfectly calibrated classifier would produce a metric value of zero over a hypothetical infinite-sized dataset) [7]. As with the Brier score, NLL is strictly proper and can be decomposed into reliability, resolution, and uncertainty [74].

claims.claim: Kernel/KDE-based calibration estimators outperform bin-based metrics on the rate of decline of mean-squared error with sample size — i.e. at the finite sample sizes of a trade journal (hundreds to thousands of entries), a KDE calibration estimator is measurably more efficient than binned ECE.
claims.quote: Among the disadvantages of bin-based metrics are the arbitrary grouping of data points into bins, and discrete jumps between bins. Kernel-based metrics seek to obtain a smooth calibration curve based on a locally weighted sum of the data points. ... Kernel estimates generally perform better than bin-based metrics on various criteria, such as rate of decline of mean-squared error with sample size [17].

claims.claim: Binned calibration error is not a fixed quantity: it increases monotonically with bin count, true calibration is unmeasurable with finitely many bins, and on FINITE datasets ECE can go either way (under- or over-estimate). So any single reported ECE number is an artifact of the bin choice and cannot be compared across models unless bin scheme and N are held fixed.
claims.quote: A general problem with bin-based schemes is that the true calibration is unmeasurable with a finite number of bins. As the number of bins is increased, the measured calibration error increases [38]. It is also the case that any binned version of calibration error underestimates the true calibration error in the limit of infinite data. However, for finite data sets ECE can under or overestimate the calibration error [67].

claims.claim: Order flow adds only marginal predictive value over a pure L2 book-shape baseline for 1m/5m state transitions in BTC/ETH perps: pooled overlay improvement was +0.010 vs a flow-shuffle null 95th percentile of +0.004 (1m) / +0.003 (5m) — i.e. barely above noise, and for BTC no regime cleared the flow test at both horizons.
claims.quote: for BTC no regime clears the corresponding order-flow tests at both horizons

claims.claim: The pre-event L2 liquidity state (spread, top-20 depth, top-20 imbalance) is a stronger predictor than order flow, improving over the marginal baseline by +0.034 (1m) and +0.045 (5m) — roughly 3-4x the order-flow overlay's +0.010.
claims.quote: the pre-event L2 liquidity state is the primary predictive object

claims.claim: Order-flow predictive power is state-dependent and concentrates in stressed liquidity regimes: for ETH the 1-minute overlay increment rises monotonically from +0.004 (calm) to +0.020 (mixed) to +0.038 (stressed), implying entry snapshots must record the liquidity regime to condition on it.
claims.quote: rises monotonically from calm to mixed to stressed

claims.claim: Absolute predictability of L2 state transitions at 1-5 minute horizons is low: the L2-shape model reached 0.586 (1m) and 0.554 (5m) classification accuracy against majority base rates of 0.571 and 0.532 — an edge of only ~1.5-2.2 percentage points over always guessing the majority class.
claims.quote: 0.586 at one minute and 0.554 at five minutes

claims.claim: Validation used rolling monthly out-of-sample folds with event-clustered validation and a permutation null with feature shuffling blocked by month, symbol, and pre-event state — a concrete blocked-permutation protocol for testing whether an order-flow feature beats chance, over 47,513 windows per horizon.
claims.quote: 47,513 windows per horizon, 18,631 of them event windows (BTC 9,330, ETH 9,301)

claims.claim: Order imbalance measured at quarter-hour clock openings forecasts crypto perpetual-futures returns at a 4-to-12-hour horizon — i.e. order-flow predictive power in this study lives at multi-hour, not second- or minute-scale, horizons, and is conditional on clock phase.
claims.quote: This opening activity is not only predictable out of sample but also informative: its order imbalance forecasts four-to-twelve-hour returns, weaker at finer marks.

claims.claim: Predictive power of order imbalance is strongest at quarter-hour marks and monotonically weaker at finer clock marks (one- and five-minute), implying that time-of-clock phase must be recorded at entry as a conditioning variable for any order-flow alpha.
claims.quote: its order imbalance forecasts four-to-twelve-hour returns, weaker at finer marks

claims.claim: Binance perpetual contracts exhibit periodic bursts in volatility and volume at one-, five-, and quarter-hour marks, so unconditional pooling of order-flow features across clock phases mixes structurally different regimes.
claims.quote: Cryptocurrency markets exhibit periodic bursts in volatility and volume at one-, five-, and quarter-hour marks.

claims.claim: The periodic bursts are attributable to algorithmic participation, identified via a decline in trade-size roundness within the bursts — making trade-size roundness a recordable, cheap proxy for algo participation at entry.
claims.quote: we associate these bursts with algorithmic trading: trade-size roundness declines sharply within them, a behavioral signature of algorithmic participation

claims.claim: Conventional (non-phase-resolved) autocorrelation measures conceal the serial dependence in order flow and returns that exists at quarter-hour openings, meaning standard time-series diagnostics will fail to detect this effect.
claims.quote: The Autocorrelation Map, a clock-phase-resolved display, reveals serial dependence in order flow and returns at the quarter-hour openings that conventional measures conceal.

claims.claim: Selecting strategy configurations by in-sample optimization score carries a measured 58.6% probability of backtest overfitting (CSCV/PBO), even when strict t+1 execution and realistic costs are already enforced — i.e. strict semantics and cost realism do NOT rescue a score-ranked gate, which is the exact failure mode of an in-sample-Sharpe selector over 142 strategies.
claims.quote: The resulting PBO estimate in our BTC snapshot is materially above zero (PBO= 0.586 under a standard 8-segment CSCV design with 70 combinatorial splits over the top-40 Stage I candidates), indicating that data-snooping risk remains substantial even under strict execution and realistic cost modeling. These diagnostics are used defensively and are not interpreted as proof of persistent alpha.

claims.claim: On BTC/USDT 4h perps with parameters held fixed, a fee-only cost model inflates annualized return from 2.726 to 4.308 (CAGR, decimal; +58%) and Sharpe from 2.049 to 2.506 versus a fully costed run including slippage and funding; a zero-cost run inflates further to 5.225 CAGR / 2.711 Sharpe. Net-edge estimation must therefore charge fees AND slippage AND funding carry, not fees alone.
claims.quote: Variant Ann. (CAGR, dec.) Sharpe MaxDD Trades / Rigorous (fees+slippage+funding) 2.726 2.049 0.265 636 / Standard (fee-only) 4.308 2.506 0.262 636 / Naive (zero-cost, upper bound) 5.225 2.711 0.260 535

claims.claim: The effective number of trials for a deflated-Sharpe adjustment must count window re-evaluations and cost-scenario evaluations as selection degrees of freedom, not just the optimizer trials: 40 configs x 9 windows x 9 cost scenarios yields Ntotal in [360, 3240], and after that deflation the flagship configuration's long-window Sharpe provides no evidence against a zero-true-Sharpe null.
claims.quote: we approximate the total number of effective trials as Ntotal ∈ [Nopt ×Nwindows, Nopt ×Nwindows ×Nscen] ... yielding Ntotal ∈ [360, 3240]. ... In the current reproducible snapshot, the long-window Sharpe is close to zero, and the DSR-style diagnostic does not suggest that Sharpe alone provides strong evidence against a zero-true-Sharpe null after accounting for multiple trials.

claims.claim: This paper contributes NOTHING to the microstructure-alpha, labeling, or entry-snapshot portions of the question: its entire empirical result set is generated from 4-hour OHLCV plus an 8-hour funding series only — no order book, no trade-level flow, no OI, no liquidations — and the framework explicitly refuses to generate or evaluate predictive signals.
claims.quote: both Stage I tuning and Stage II screening are reproduced from the standardized 4-hour (4h) OHLCV (Open, High, Low, Close, Volume) series together with the aligned 8-hour funding series under STRICT4H semantics; no auxiliary 1m/15m inputs are required to regenerate the reported Stage I/II tables and figures.

claims.claim: Contrary to the common assumption that same-bar (t+0) execution universally inflates backtest results, across the top-30 Stage I trials on BTC/USDT 4h the median NAIVE-minus-STRICT uplift in annualized return was -0.018 with only 36.7% of trials showing positive uplift — so look-ahead-in-execution is not the source of the score/profit gap; selection bias is.
claims.quote: the median uplift (NAIVE minus STRICT) in annualized return is negative and the fraction of trials with positive uplift is below 50%, indicating that naive same-bar execution does not act as a universal performance booster in this setting.
